prompt.context: Our client, Wildcats Lacrosse, is a leading US sporting goods company. They manufacture, market and sell two primary products: 1) women's lacrosse masks, 2) women's lacrosse sticks. They sell these products exclusively to the US market. Wildcat masks sell very well and are the market leader. Their lacrosse sticks, on the other hand, do not sell well despite Wildcats' best efforts. Wildcats is worried that they are missing out on an opportunity with their lacrosse sticks. They have discussed a number of options including discontinuing the sticks and instead focusing on making only masks.
prompt.question: They would like to better understand their options and have come to us for guidance. Investigate the comparative profitability of both products and develop a plan to determine whether Wildcats should keep producing sticks and how overall profitability of the firm can be improved.

clarifying_info.a: We can assume little to no market growth.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been new entrants or substitutes in the market?
clarifying_info.a: No new entrants into the markets for either masks or sticks; the products are not substitutes for one another.

clarifying_info.q: Has Wildcats' market share changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: Wildcats has not seen its market share change in the near term and expects it to be steady into the future.

clarifying_info.q: Do we have price elasticity data?
clarifying_info.a: Wildcats does not have any information on price elasticity.

clarifying_info.q: How does Wildcats price its products?
clarifying_info.a: Wildcats uses a cost-plus pricing scheme — 10% above total cost.

clarifying_info.q: Does Wildcats have capacity to increase production?
clarifying_info.a: Wildcats has a single manufacturing facility; assume there is some reasonable utilization rate below 100% to allow for some production increases without the need for capex.

clarifying_info.q: What is included in variable costs?
clarifying_info.a: Variable costs include transportation and logistics.

clarifying_info.q: What are the characteristics of the mask product?
clarifying_info.a: Masks are very equipment-intensive, have high R&D spend, change rapidly, and must meet stringent safety requirements.

clarifying_info.q: What are the characteristics of the stick product?
clarifying_info.a: Sticks are very labor-intensive (stringing the pocket is time-consuming and requires skill), have fairly low R&D spend, fairly long product life cycles, and high quality expectations. Wildcats sources the shaft from a third party and completes final painting in-house.

clarifying_info.q: Can Wildcats sell everything it produces?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, Wildcats is able to sell all products that they manufacture.

exhibits.title: Production Costs (USD)
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart comparing per-unit production costs for Masks vs Sticks, split between variable costs and fixed costs (allocated by labor hours per part).

exhibits.title: Fixed Costs Allocation Based on Capital Spending (USD, k)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing total fixed costs and their breakdown between masks, sticks, and shared, based on actual capital spending rather than labor hours.

exhibits.title: Annual Production Volumes
exhibits.shows: A chart showing Wildcats' annual production volumes for masks and sticks.

framework: Profitability = Revenue - Costs for each product line (Masks and Sticks)
Revenue: Price × Volume; understand pricing strategy (cost-plus at 10% markup)
Costs: Split into fixed costs (PP&E, R&D, overhead) and variable costs (materials, labor, logistics)
Fixed cost allocation: examine whether current allocation method (labor hours) accurately reflects actual resource consumption
Competitive context: market share, pricing vs. competitors, price sensitivity
Strategic options: discontinue sticks, change pricing strategy, change cost allocation approach, optimize overall profitability

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what do you observe about the production costs of masks vs. sticks?
questions.guidance: Both fixed and variable costs of sticks are roughly 5x those of masks. Masks: $3 VC + $2 FC = $5 total. Sticks: $15 VC + $10 FC = $25 total. Fixed costs in Exhibit 1 are allocated by labor hours per part.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, how does the capital-spending-based fixed cost allocation differ from the labor-hour-based allocation? Calculate the new per-unit fixed costs and total per-unit costs using capital spending allocation (assume 50/50 split for shared costs).
questions.guidance: Masks drive most capital spending (equipment-intensive, high R&D, safety requirements). Under capital-based allocation, the overhead burden shifts significantly away from sticks and toward masks. Key insight: sticks are labor-intensive but not capital-intensive.

math.setup: Total FC = $1,000k. Masks capital FC = $600k, Sticks capital FC = $300k, Shared = $100k. Allocate shared 50/50: Masks OH = $600k + $50k = $650k; Sticks OH = $300k + $50k = $350k. Divide by units (from Exhibit 3): Masks 250k units, Sticks 50k units.
steps: Masks total cost = $3.00 VC + $2.60 FC = $5.60 (vs. old $5.00; +12%)
Sticks total cost = $15.00 VC + $7.00 FC = $22.00 (vs. old $25.00; -12%)
math.answer: Under capital-based allocation, Masks cost $5.60/unit and Sticks cost $22.00/unit.

questions.prompt: What challenges arise when switching to activity-based cost allocation?
questions.guidance: Strong answers mention: (1) difficulty tracking activities accurately, (2) data quality issues, (3) sensitivity to changes in production volume (overhead per unit shifts as volume changes), (4) this reallocation does not change the firm's total profitability — it only changes how costs are attributed to each product; better transparency into true product profitability is the key benefit.

questions.prompt: Calculate revenue and profit for both products under the original cost structure (cost-plus at 10% markup, original costs).
questions.guidance: Using original cost figures from Exhibit 1 and 10% cost-plus pricing. Both products yield equal revenue and equal profit, which is counter-intuitive and should prompt further investigation.

math.setup: Price = Cost × 1.10. Masks: cost = $5.00, price = $5.50. Sticks: cost = $25.00, price = $27.50. Volumes from Exhibit 3: 250k masks, 50k sticks.
math.answer: Both Masks and Sticks each generate $1.375m in revenue and $125k in profit — equally profitable despite very different volumes and costs.

questions.prompt: If Wildcats adopts the new capital-based cost allocation and maintains its 10% cost-plus pricing strategy, what should the new prices be?
questions.guidance: Apply 10% markup to revised costs. Masks price rises; sticks price falls. This creates important competitive implications: masks were already the cheapest in the market at $5.50, and sticks were priced above most competitors.

math.setup: New costs: Masks = $5.60, Sticks = $22.00. Apply 10% markup.
math.answer: New Masks price = $6.16; new Sticks price = $24.20.

questions.prompt: Estimate the impact on market share and volume if Wildcats adopts the new prices. What happens to overall profitability?
questions.guidance: Raising mask price from $5.50 to $6.16 likely reduces Wildcats' market share (masks market: Wildcats 50%→40%, Blue Devils 20%→25%, Quakers 30%→35%). Lowering stick price from $27.50 to $24.20 increases Wildcats' stick market share (Wildcats 20%→26%, Quakers 30%→28%, Terrapins 50%→46%). Candidate should recognize total Wildcats volume decreases, which increases overhead per unit — this effect should be flagged even if directed to ignore it for calculation purposes.

math.setup: Market size: Masks total 500k units, Sticks total 250k units. New volumes: Masks Wildcats 40%×500k=200k; Sticks Wildcats 26%×250k=65k. Profit = (price - VC - FC_per_unit) × volume, using revised costs.
math.answer: Total profitability improves modestly from $250k to $255k. The gain on sticks ($143k vs $125k) partially offsets the loss on masks ($112k vs $125k).

questions.prompt: Is there a better pricing strategy than cost-plus? Estimate the upside if Wildcats raises mask prices independently of cost.
questions.guidance: Wildcats masks are significantly cheaper than competitors (Blue Devils $7.50, Quakers $7.00) even at the new $6.16 price. This suggests pricing power. Wildcats could raise mask prices toward competitor levels without necessarily losing market leadership. Even a conservative volume decline leaves substantially higher profit.

math.setup: Assume Wildcats raises mask price to $7.00 with 35% market share (conservative estimate). Original cost structure variable costs $5.00 used as cost basis for illustration.
steps: Profit = ($7.00 - $5.00) × 175k = $2.00 × 175k = $350k (but casebook uses $5.50 original VC+FC as reference)
math.answer: Raising mask price to $7.00 with conservative 35% share yields ~$262.5k in mask profit vs. original $125k — more than doubling mask profitability.

brainstorming.prompt: What challenges might arise from switching to an activity-based cost allocation system, and what are the broader strategic levers Wildcats could pull to improve overall profitability?

categories.name: Cost Allocation Challenges
ideas: Difficulty accurately tracking activities and time spent per product
Data quality and reliability of internal records
Overhead per unit fluctuates with production volume changes
Implementation cost and organizational change management
Accounting and reporting system changes required

categories.name: Pricing Strategy Levers
ideas: Abandon cost-plus in favor of value-based or competitive pricing
Test price elasticity before committing to major price changes
Consider premium pricing for masks given safety and brand differentiation
Use competitive benchmarking (Blue Devils at $7.50, Quakers at $7.00) to identify pricing headroom for masks
Explore dynamic or tiered pricing

categories.name: Cost Reduction Opportunities
ideas: Renegotiate third-party shaft sourcing contracts for sticks
Invest in automation to reduce labor intensity of stick production (stringing)
Consolidate R&D spend across product lines
Reduce variable logistics costs through better route optimization
Explore shared manufacturing efficiencies

categories.name: Revenue Growth Levers
ideas: Expand product line (accessories, apparel, equipment)
Enter adjacent markets (men's lacrosse, other women's sports)
Grow international distribution
Strengthen brand loyalty to support premium pricing
Consider e-commerce and direct-to-consumer channel

categories.name: Strategic Options for Sticks
ideas: Keep sticks — they are actually profitable under correct cost allocation
Invest to grow stick market share given lower competitive prices post-reallocation
Consider outsourcing stick stringing to reduce labor cost
Explore partnership or licensing arrangements for stick production

recommendation: Do not discontinue lacrosse sticks — under a more accurate capital-based cost allocation, sticks are equally profitable to masks ($125k each) and become more profitable when priced correctly under the new cost structure
Revise the cost allocation methodology from labor-hour-based to capital-spending-based to better reflect actual resource consumption and make informed product decisions

Reevaluate the cost-plus pricing strategy: masks have significant pricing headroom relative to competitors (Blue Devils $7.50, Quakers $7.00) — raising mask prices toward market rates could substantially increase profitability
risks: Raising mask prices may reduce market share and volume if customers are price-sensitive or switch to competitors
Switching cost allocation methods requires reliable data tracking and may face internal resistance
Lowering stick prices to increase share may trigger a competitive price response from Quakers and Terrapins
Total overhead per unit increases if overall production volume falls
next_steps: Conduct price elasticity analysis for both masks and sticks before finalizing any pricing changes
Implement activity-based costing system with proper data infrastructure
Analyze stick stringing labor costs in detail to identify potential automation or outsourcing savings
Model multiple pricing scenarios with sensitivity analysis to identify the optimal price point for masks
Track competitive response to any pricing moves
